lessons.title: The Four Humours & Supernatural
lessons.description: The Four Humours, Hippocrates, Galen’s Theory of Opposites, and supernatural beliefs about illness in the medieval world.
lessons.content_html:
Introduction: How Did People Explain Disease?

For most of history, nobody understood what caused disease. Without microscopes or modern science, doctors relied on observation, philosophy, and religion to explain illness. The ideas they came up with — from the Four Humours to supernatural explanations — dominated medicine for over a thousand years.

This lesson covers the key ideas about disease in the ancient and medieval periods: the work of Hippocrates and Galen, supernatural beliefs, and the role of astrology in diagnosis.

Hippocrates & the Theory of the Four Humours

Hippocrates (c.460–370 BC) was an Ancient Greek physician often called the “Father of Medicine.” Before him, most Greeks believed illness was a punishment from the gods. Hippocrates argued that disease had natural causes and looked for physical explanations instead.

Key Fact — The Four Humours

Hippocrates believed the body contained four main fluids, or “humours”:

  • Blood — linked to spring, air, and a hot & wet nature
  • Yellow Bile — linked to summer, fire, and a hot & dry nature
  • Black Bile — linked to autumn, earth, and a cold & dry nature
  • Phlegm — linked to winter, water, and a cold & wet nature

If these humours were perfectly balanced, the person was healthy. If one became too dominant, they fell ill.

Hippocrates’ Approach: Clinical Observation

Hippocrates also promoted clinical observation — carefully watching patients, recording symptoms, and tracking how illness progressed. This pushed doctors towards evidence and reason rather than prayers or rituals.

He compiled medical texts known as the Hippocratic Corpus, covering diagnosis, treatment, surgery, and the role of diet and exercise. These texts were studied for centuries and became the foundation of Western medical training.

Key Fact — The Hippocratic Oath

The Hippocratic Oath is a set of ethical rules for doctors attributed to Hippocrates. It included promises to treat patients to the best of one’s ability, do no harm, and keep patient information private. Versions of this oath are still used by doctors today.

Galen & the Theory of Opposites

Galen (c.129–216 AD) was a Roman physician of Greek origin. He studied anatomy in Egypt by examining dead bodies and bones, then spent 15 years as a doctor at a gladiator school — giving him rare hands-on experience of injuries and wound treatment. He built on Hippocrates’ ideas by developing the Theory of Opposites: if a patient had too much of one humour, treat them with the “opposite” quality to restore balance.

Galen also proved that the brain, not the heart, controlled the body by cutting a pig’s spinal cord at different points. However, because he dissected animals rather than humans, many of his anatomical observations contained errors that went unchallenged for centuries.

Key Fact — Theory of Opposites in Practice

A fever (too much blood — hot & wet) would be treated with something cold or dry. A cold (too much phlegm — cold & wet) would be treated with pepper or hot spices. This gave doctors a logical system for choosing treatments, even though the theory itself was wrong.

Key Fact — Treating Each Humour

Each humour had a specific treatment designed to remove or reduce it when in excess:

  • Too much blood → bleeding (using cups or leeches to draw blood out)
  • Too much yellow bile → vomiting, induced by giving the patient emetics
  • Too much black bile → purging, using laxatives to empty the bowels
  • Too much phlegm → warming and sweating the patient to dry out the excess moisture

Why Did Galen’s Ideas Last So Long?

Galen’s ideas dominated European medicine for over 1,500 years. Why did they last so long?

Volume of writing: Galen produced over 350 books on anatomy, disease, and treatment. His work became the standard reference across Europe and the Islamic world.

Church support: Galen believed the body was perfectly designed, which fitted the Christian belief that God created humans. The Church promoted his work — challenging Galen meant challenging the Church.

No way to check: The Church banned human dissection for much of the medieval period, so nobody could test whether Galen’s descriptions were correct. Many were based on animal dissections and contained serious errors.

Collapse of the Roman Empire: After Rome fell in 410 AD, much knowledge was lost. The texts that survived — often preserved by Islamic scholars — were treated with huge respect. Few dared question the ancients.

Supernatural Beliefs About Disease

Although Hippocrates and Galen promoted natural explanations, supernatural beliefs remained very common throughout the medieval period. For most ordinary people — and for the Church — disease was linked to religion.

God’s Punishment

The most common supernatural explanation was that disease was a punishment from God for sinful behaviour. The Bible described God sending plagues to punish the wicked, and medieval people took this literally. If someone fell ill, it was often assumed they had angered God.

If disease came from God, the logical cure was a religious one: prayer, repentance, fasting, pilgrimage, or donating to the Church. Sick people visited holy shrines, prayed to healing saints, or touched sacred relics hoping to be cured.

Key Fact

Because people believed God sent disease, the Church played a central role in healthcare. Priests were often consulted before doctors, and prayer and pilgrimage were among the most common “treatments.”

The Role of Astrology in Diagnosis

Astrology played a major role in medieval medicine. Physicians consulted zodiac charts to diagnose illness and decide when to treat patients, believing the stars and planets could affect the balance of humours.

Different zodiac signs were linked to different body parts — Aries to the head, Pisces to the feet. A doctor might refuse to perform bloodletting if the stars were not in a favourable position. Even university-trained physicians were expected to understand astrology.

Without microscopes, there was no way to see germs. People noticed disease could spread and seemed linked to the seasons, but had no scientific way to explain why. Supernatural and astrological explanations made sense with the knowledge available.

The Church reinforced these beliefs. It controlled education, universities, and most books, so ideas that contradicted religious teaching were suppressed. Most people were illiterate and relied on their priest to explain the world.

Key Individuals: A Timeline

c.460–370 BC

Hippocrates

Developed the Four Humours theory, promoted clinical observation, and argued disease had natural — not supernatural — causes. Credited with the Hippocratic Oath.

c.129–216 AD

Galen

Built on Hippocrates with the Theory of Opposites. Wrote over 350 books. His ideas were promoted by the Church and dominated European medicine for 1,500+ years.

Medieval Period (c.500–1500)

Supernatural beliefs dominate

Most people still believed disease was sent by God as punishment. Astrology, prayer, and pilgrimage remained central to medical practice.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about the Four Humours, link it to bigger themes: observation vs. religion, why ideas stayed the same for so long (Church support, no technology, respect for ancients), and how the Renaissance later challenged them. Strong answers show continuity and change.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

The Four Humours was one of the earliest attempts to explain how the body works. Although it was wrong, it was a key shift towards natural — rather than supernatural — explanations for disease. Yet supernatural beliefs stayed central to everyday medicine throughout the medieval period.

Key Takeaways

  • Hippocrates introduced natural explanations: The Four Humours said illness came from imbalanced bodily fluids, not the gods. His focus on clinical observation laid the groundwork for evidence-based medicine.
  • Galen dominated for 1,500+ years: Church support, dissection bans, and the sheer volume of his writing made his ideas almost impossible to challenge — even the errors.
  • Supernatural beliefs coexisted with rational medicine: Even educated doctors used astrology alongside the Four Humours. For most people, prayer and pilgrimage came first. This mix of rational and supernatural thinking is key for the exam.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the treatments used by medieval doctors.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain the significance
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of aspects of significance. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Students move from developed explanation by explaining the relationship between aspects of significance, for example over time.
Example: Medieval treatments such as bloodletting, purging, and herbal remedies were significant because they were all based on the Theory of the Four Humours. This meant that for over 1,000 years, the approach to treating illness did not fundamentally change — doctors continued to try to rebalance the humours rather than targeting the actual cause of disease. The significance extends over time because Galen’s Theory of Opposites gave these treatments a logical framework that the Church endorsed, making them almost impossible to challenge until the Renaissance.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of aspects of significance. Students move from simple explanation by developed reasoning considering two or more aspects of significance.
Example: Bloodletting was significant because it was the most common treatment for nearly every condition, using methods like venesection, leeches, and cupping. Herbal remedies were also significant because some, like willow bark (containing salicin, related to aspirin) and honey (a natural antiseptic), had genuine medical value — showing that medieval medicine was not entirely useless.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of one aspect of significance. Students move from basic explanation by simple reasoning of one identified aspect.
Example: Bloodletting was significant because it was based on the idea that excess blood caused illness. Doctors used leeches or cut veins to remove blood and try to restore the balance of humours.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of aspect(s) of significance. Students identify aspect(s) relevant to the question. Explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Medieval doctors used bloodletting and herbal remedies to treat illness.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which ideas about the causes of disease in Ancient Greece and ideas about the causes of disease in the medieval period were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain two similarities
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of similarities. Students move from developed explanation by explaining complexities of similarities arising from the broader historical context.
Example: Both periods relied on the Theory of the Four Humours as the main natural explanation for disease, and both also used supernatural explanations alongside it. This continuity existed because Galen’s writings (building on Hippocrates) were promoted by the Christian Church, which controlled education and banned challenges to accepted ideas. The lack of technology such as microscopes meant neither period could identify the real causes of disease, so the same theories persisted for over 1,500 years.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of similarities. Students move from simple explanation by developed reasoning considering two or more identified similarities.
Example: In both periods, the Theory of the Four Humours was the main explanation for disease. Ancient Greek physicians like Hippocrates argued that illness was caused by an imbalance in blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm, and medieval doctors still used the same theory over 1,000 years later, diagnosing patients using urine charts. Both periods also relied on supernatural explanations: the Greeks blamed the gods, while medieval people believed God sent disease as punishment for sin.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of one similarity. Students move from basic explanation by reasoning supported with factual knowledge.
Example: Both periods believed in the Theory of the Four Humours. In Ancient Greece, Hippocrates said disease was caused by an imbalance of the four fluids, and medieval doctors still used this idea to diagnose illness.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of similarity/similarities. Students identify similarity/similarities relevant to the question. Explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Both periods believed illness was caused by the four humours.

practice_questions.text: Has religion been the main factor in the development of medicine in Britain since Medieval times? Explain your answer with reference to religion and other factors. Use a range of examples from across your study of Health and the people: c1000 to the present day.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks (+4 SPaG) — Has religion been the main factor?
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (13-16): Complex explanation of stated factor and other factor(s) leading to sustained judgement. Range of accurate and detailed knowledge. Complex, sustained line of reasoning, sharply focused and fully substantiated. Students develop by analysis of relationship between factors.

This prevented progress for centuries. However, over the full time period, science and technology became the dominant factor. Pasteur’s germ theory (1861) only became possible through microscope technology, and modern breakthroughs like DNA sequencing and keyhole surgery depend entirely on technology. Religion’s role shifted from hindrance to irrelevance as science took over. lessons.title: Medieval Treatments & the Church
lessons.description: How the Church both helped and hindered medicine, monastery care, and the contributions of Islamic scholars like Rhazes and Avicenna.
lessons.content_html:
The Christian Church & Medieval Medicine

In the Middle Ages, the Christian Church was very powerful and controlled almost every part of life, including medicine. It ran the universities where doctors trained, decided which books could be studied, and shaped how ordinary people understood illness. The Church taught that God sent illness as a punishment for sin or as a test of faith.

Religious remedies — prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, and repentance — were often the first response to illness. However, the Church also provided the only organised care for the sick and poor in medieval Britain.

Medieval people also believed in miasma — the idea that “bad air” caused disease. Foul-smelling vapours from rotting matter, swamps, and sewage were thought to enter the body and make people ill. This belief lasted for centuries, influencing public health into the 19th century. During plague outbreaks, people carried posies of flowers or sweet herbs to ward off the “poisonous” air.

Medieval Hospitals

The Church was the main provider of hospital care in medieval Britain. By 1500, there were over 1,200 hospitals across the country. These were very different from modern hospitals — their purpose was to care for the sick, not cure them. Most were small and attached to monasteries or run by religious orders. Only around 10% actually cared for the sick. The rest offered “hospitality” in its original sense: a place to rest, eat, and pray, not receive medical treatment.

Key Fact — Medieval Hospitals
  • Run by monks, nuns, or religious orders — not trained doctors
  • Provided food, shelter, warmth, and prayer for the sick and poor
  • Rarely attempted to treat or cure diseases
  • Often refused entry to patients with infectious diseases to protect other residents
  • The focus was on spiritual care: patients were encouraged to pray and confess their sins

Monastery Sanitation

Monks had the knowledge, money, and discipline to create much better public health systems than towns had. Monasteries had excellent water supplies and built latrines to carry away sewage, keeping their water source separate from waste. They also had infirmaries for sick monks and herb gardens to grow plants for remedies.

This made monasteries some of the cleanest and healthiest places in medieval Britain. Regular washing, clean water, and organised waste disposal put them far ahead of most towns.

Monastery herb gardens were an important source of remedies. One example is foxglove, used to treat “feebleness of the heart.” A chemical from foxglove called digitalis is still used in modern medicine for heart conditions — one of the clearest examples of a medieval remedy with real scientific value.

The Church: Help or Hindrance?

A key exam theme is whether the Church helped or hindered medical progress. The answer is both — and a strong answer shows this balance.

By 1300, there were fewer than 100 trained physicians in all of England. Most ordinary people could never afford one and instead relied on local healers, wise women, or the Church for their healthcare.

Roger Bacon, a 13th-century Franciscan friar, argued that doctors should carry out experiments rather than just relying on Galen. For challenging Church teaching, he was arrested and imprisoned — a clear warning to anyone who dared question accepted ideas.

Exam Tip

For questions about the Church’s role, you must give a balanced argument. Explain both the positive contributions and the negative effects. The strongest answers reach a judgement on whether the Church did more to help or hinder — and back it up with specific evidence.

Islamic Medicine

While Europe was in the “Dark Ages” after the fall of Rome, the Islamic world was in a golden age of learning. Islamic scholars translated, preserved, and built upon Greek and Roman medical texts — especially Hippocrates and Galen. Without them, much of this knowledge would have been lost forever.

The Islamic faith actively encouraged learning. The Quran taught that Muslims had a duty to care for the sick and seek cures. Medicine was valued and funded across the Islamic world, leading to major advances.

Rhazes (al-Razi, c.854–925 AD)

Rhazes (also known as al-Razi) was a Persian physician who made several breakthroughs. He was the first doctor to clearly distinguish between smallpox and measles — two diseases previously confused. He did this through careful clinical observation, recording each disease’s symptoms in detail.

Rhazes wrote over 200 medical texts and ran a hospital in Baghdad. He used clinical observation in the tradition of Hippocrates — carefully watching patients and recording symptoms rather than just relying on ancient texts.

Ibn Sina / Avicenna (c.980–1037 AD)

Ibn Sina (known in Europe as Avicenna) was perhaps the most influential Islamic physician. His masterwork, The Canon of Medicine, compiled and organised all known medical knowledge from the Greek, Roman, and Islamic traditions.

Key Fact — The Canon of Medicine

Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine was translated into Latin and became the standard medical textbook in European universities for over 500 years. It covered topics including the properties of drugs, the diagnosis and treatment of diseases, and the importance of diet, exercise, and hygiene. It contained descriptions of over 760 different drugs and their effects.

Ibn al-Nafis (c.1213–1288 AD)

Ibn al-Nafis was a Syrian physician who criticised Galen’s ideas about how blood moved through the body. Galen claimed blood was made in the liver, “burned up” by the organs, and passed between the two sides of the heart through invisible pores. Ibn al-Nafis rejected this. He correctly argued that blood circulated around the body and passed through the lungs — centuries before William Harvey proved full circulation in 1628.

Islamic Contributions to Pharmacy

Islamic scholars also made major advances in pharmacy. Through alchemy, they developed techniques like distillation to create purer, more effective medicines. They set up the first dedicated pharmacies and developed systems for testing and cataloguing drugs.

These advances fed back into European medicine when Islamic texts were translated into Latin, especially in Spain and Sicily. The knowledge Islamic scholars preserved and advanced was essential to the medical breakthroughs of the European Renaissance.

The Crusades & Knowledge Transfer

The Crusades (holy wars from 1095) brought thousands of Europeans into direct contact with Islamic medicine. Returning crusaders brought back medical knowledge, herbs, and surgical techniques far more advanced than anything in Europe. This was one of the key ways Islamic medical knowledge reached the West.

Usamah ibn Munqidh (1095–1188), a Muslim writer, recorded a striking story. An Arab doctor was treating a knight’s infected leg with clean dressings — and it was healing well. A European doctor arrived, dismissed the approach, and insisted on amputation. The knight died. The same European doctor then cut open a woman’s skull to treat her. She also died.

This story — told from a Muslim perspective — shows how far behind European surgery was compared to the Islamic world. It is useful evidence for exam answers about Islamic medicine’s contribution.

Religious encouragement: The Quran encouraged Muslims to seek knowledge and care for the sick — unlike the Christian Church’s focus on disease as God’s punishment.

Wealth and stability: The Islamic Empire was wealthy and stable. Rulers funded hospitals, libraries, and centres of learning. The great library at Baghdad, the House of Wisdom, attracted scholars from across the world.

Translation movement: Islamic scholars translated Greek and Roman texts into Arabic, preserving knowledge being lost in post-Roman Europe. They did not just copy these texts — they critiqued, corrected, and expanded them.

Practical emphasis: European medicine focused on theory and ancient authority. Islamic physicians placed greater emphasis on observation, experimentation, and practical results.

Key Individuals: A Timeline

c.854–925 AD

Rhazes (al-Razi)

Persian physician who first distinguished between smallpox and measles. Wrote over 200 medical texts and ran a hospital in Baghdad using clinical observation.

c.980–1037 AD

Ibn Sina (Avicenna)

Wrote The Canon of Medicine, a vast encyclopaedia used as Europe’s main medical textbook for over 500 years. Catalogued over 760 drugs.

c.1213–1288 AD

Ibn al-Nafis

Syrian physician who challenged Galen’s ideas about blood, correctly arguing that blood circulated through the lungs rather than passing through invisible pores in the heart. Anticipated Harvey by over 300 years.

By 1500

Over 1,200 hospitals in England

The Church had established a vast network of hospitals across medieval Britain, though their focus was on spiritual care rather than medical cure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about the Church’s role, you must give a balanced argument. Explain both the positive contributions and the negative effects. The strongest answers reach a judgement on whether the Church did more to help or hinder — and back it up with specific evidence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

The Church was the backbone of medieval healthcare, providing care and building the cleanest communities in monasteries. But its control over ideas and emphasis on supernatural causes of disease also blocked scientific progress. Meanwhile, Islamic scholars preserved and advanced ancient medical knowledge, making breakthroughs that would later help transform European medicine.

Key Takeaways

  • The Church both helped and hindered medicine: It provided hospitals, preserved texts, and built clean monasteries — but also banned dissection, promoted Galen uncritically, and encouraged belief in supernatural cures. Show this balance for top marks.
  • Islamic scholars preserved and advanced ancient knowledge: Rhazes, Ibn Sina, and Ibn al-Nafis translated Greek and Roman texts, corrected errors, and made breakthroughs in observation, pharmacy, and blood circulation.
  • Medieval hospitals were about care, not cure: They provided food, shelter, and prayer, but rarely attempted medical treatment.

lessons.title: Medieval Surgery & Hospitals
lessons.description: Bloodletting, purging, herbal remedies, and the brutal world of barber surgeons facing pain, infection and bleeding.
lessons.content_html:
Diagnosis in the Medieval Period

Medieval physicians believed illness was caused by an imbalance in the Four Humours. To work out which humour was off balance, they used two main tools: a urine chart and a zodiac chart.

The physician examined the patient’s urine — checking its colour, smell, and even taste — and compared it to the chart to spot the imbalance. They then checked the zodiac chart to find the best time to treat, based on the stars and planets. This mix of humoral theory and astrology was standard medical practice.

Common Medieval Treatments

Since physicians believed illness came from a humoral imbalance, treatments aimed to restore that balance. Some seem extreme today, but they were logical within humoral medicine.

Bloodletting

Bloodletting was the most common treatment for nearly every condition. It aimed to remove excess blood — the humour most often blamed for illness. There were three main methods:

Key Fact — Methods of Bloodletting
  • Venesection: Cutting open a vein with a sharp blade and draining blood into a bowl. The physician would use the zodiac chart to decide which vein to cut and when.
  • Leeches: Placing blood-sucking leeches on the patient’s skin to draw out blood more slowly and with less risk.
  • Cupping: Placing heated glass cups on the skin. As the air inside cooled, it created suction that drew blood to the surface.

Purging

To remove excess humours other than blood, patients were forced to empty their bodies. Emetics made patients vomit, while laxatives emptied the bowels. The aim was always the same: physically remove the humour thought to be causing illness.

Herbal Remedies

Local apothecaries or “wise women” created remedies from plants and minerals. Many were based on the Theory of Opposites — using a “hot” herb to treat a “cold” illness, for example. Some had real value (honey as an antiseptic, willow bark for pain — which contains a chemical related to aspirin), but many were useless or even harmful.

Some remedies worked, even though people did not understand why. Honey has natural antibacterial properties. Willow bark contains salicin, which the body converts into salicylic acid — the active ingredient in aspirin. Mint helped digestion, and garlic has proven antimicrobial properties.

But many other remedies were useless or dangerous — using ground-up gems, animal dung, or mercury. Without scientific testing, there was no way to tell effective remedies from harmful ones.

Exam Tip

Always explain why a treatment was used. Don’t just say “they performed bloodletting.” Say “they performed bloodletting because they believed excess blood was causing illness, and removing it would restore the balance of the Four Humours.” Linking treatments to the ideas behind them earns higher marks.

Medieval Surgery

Surgery was a separate craft from medicine and a last resort. It was not done by university-trained physicians but by barber surgeons — tradesmen who also cut hair and pulled teeth. Surgery was seen as lower-status: a manual craft, not an intellectual one.

The Three Problems of Surgery

Medieval surgeons faced three huge problems that made any operation very dangerous:

Key Fact — The Three Problems
  • Pain: There were no effective anaesthetics. Patients were sometimes given alcohol or a sponge soaked in opium to dull the pain, but these were unreliable. Many patients went into shock or moved during surgery, making precise work impossible.
  • Infection: With no understanding of germs, surgical instruments were not sterilised and surgeons did not wash their hands. Wounds frequently became infected after operations, and many patients died from infection rather than the original injury.
  • Bleeding: Surgeons had no reliable way to stop heavy bleeding during or after operations. Without the ability to transfuse blood or effectively seal blood vessels, patients could easily bleed to death during even minor procedures.

“Laudable Pus”

Many surgeons believed that pus forming in a wound was a good sign — proof the body was healing by expelling harmful humours. They called this “laudable pus”. In reality, pus is a clear sign of infection. This meant surgeons often took no steps to prevent infection — and sometimes encouraged it, with fatal results.

Key Named Surgeons

Although surgery was seen as a lower craft, several individuals pushed surgical knowledge forward:

Key Fact — Abulcasis (Albucasis, c.936–1013)

Abulcasis was an Islamic surgeon from Cordoba in Muslim Spain, often called the “Father of Modern Surgery.” He wrote Al Tasrif, a 30-volume medical encyclopaedia that included detailed descriptions of surgical procedures and illustrations of instruments. He invented 26 new surgical instruments and popularised the use of cauterisation to seal wounds and stop bleeding.

Key Fact — Hugh & Theodoric of Lucca (13th century)

Hugh of Lucca and his son Theodoric worked at the University of Bologna. Crucially, they criticised the widespread belief in “laudable pus” and argued that pus was harmful, not helpful. They used wine to clean wounds and reduce infection — an idea that went against accepted medical teaching but was far closer to modern antiseptic practice.

Key Fact — John of Arderne (c.1307–1392)

John of Arderne was an English surgeon who wrote Practica, a surgical text with detailed illustrations of operations and instruments. He used opium as a pain reliever during surgery and developed a successful treatment for anal fistula — a painful condition common among knights who spent long hours on horseback. Arderne also campaigned to raise the status of surgery by separating surgeons from barbers, helping to establish the Guild of Surgeons.

What Procedures Could Be Performed?

Despite these limits, barber surgeons did carry out a range of procedures — mostly surface-level operations or emergencies where the patient would die without intervention:

Amputation: Removing a badly injured or gangrenous limb. Done quickly to limit pain and bleeding, then cauterised (sealed with a red-hot iron).

Trepanning: Drilling a hole in the skull to release evil spirits or relieve pressure. Some patients survived — we know from archaeological evidence.

Setting broken bones: Surgeons could set simple fractures and make splints. Compound fractures (bone breaking through skin) were usually fatal due to infection.

Cauterisation: Sealing wounds with a red-hot iron to stop bleeding. Very painful, but could prevent blood loss.

Pulling teeth: One of the most common procedures, since tooth decay was widespread.

At the Battle of Shrewsbury (1403), the 16-year-old Prince Henry (later Henry V) was struck in the face by an arrow. The shaft was pulled out, but the arrowhead stayed six inches deep in his skull. Surgeon John Bradmore invented a special screw-like tool to grip and extract it, saving the prince’s life. Surviving portraits of Henry V are often in profile — to hide the scar.

This case shows that medieval surgeons could achieve impressive results when necessity demanded innovation.

War as a Driver of Surgical Progress

Warfare drove surgical improvement. Most barber surgeons gained experience on the battlefield, treating sword and arrow wounds. The Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) gave over 30 years of surgical practice and pushed innovation in treating battlefield injuries. War created constant demand for practitioners who could amputate limbs, extract arrows, and cauterise wounds quickly.

Anatomy & Dissection

In 1315, public dissection was first allowed at the University of Bologna. Mondino de Luzzi wrote Anathomia, the standard dissection manual for over 200 years. But dissection was mainly used to confirm Galen’s ideas, not challenge them. The professor read from Galen while an assistant cut the body. Any differences were blamed on the body, not on Galen. It took until the Renaissance for anatomists like Vesalius to use dissection to overturn Galen’s mistakes.

Who Provided Medical Care?

Different types of practitioners provided different levels of care. Access to treatment depended heavily on wealth and social class:

Key Fact — Types of Medical Practitioners
  • Physicians: University-trained doctors who studied ancient texts. They diagnosed illness and prescribed treatments but rarely got their hands dirty. Only the wealthy could afford to consult a physician.
  • Barber surgeons: Tradesmen who performed surgery, pulled teeth, and cut hair. They learned through apprenticeships, not university training. Attempts were made to professionalise surgery and raise its status, including the formation of the Guild of Surgeons, which sought to separate trained surgeons from ordinary barbers.
  • Apothecaries: Prepared and sold herbal remedies and medicines. Similar to a modern pharmacist but without scientific training.
  • Wise women: Women in local communities who had knowledge of herbal remedies passed down through generations. Often the first point of contact for the poor.
  • The Church: Priests offered spiritual healing through prayer, and monasteries provided hospital care focused on rest and religious devotion.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Always explain why a treatment was used. Don’t just say “they performed bloodletting.” Say “they performed bloodletting because they believed excess blood was causing illness, and removing it would restore the balance of the Four Humours.” Linking treatments to the ideas behind them earns higher marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

Medieval treatments put the Theory of the Four Humours into practice, leading to bloodletting and purging. Surgery was a separate, brutal craft — barber surgeons struggled with pain, infection, and bleeding. Some herbal remedies had real value, but without scientific understanding, treatments were often useless or dangerous.

Key Takeaways

  • Treatments were based on humoral theory: Bloodletting, purging, and herbal remedies all aimed to restore the balance of the Four Humours. Always link treatments to the ideas behind them in your answers.
  • Surgery was dangerous and a last resort: Barber surgeons faced pain, infection, and bleeding. “Laudable pus” shows how the lack of germ theory made outcomes worse.
  • Access to care depended on wealth: Physicians served the rich; the poor relied on wise women, apothecaries, or the Church.

All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of similarities. Students move from developed explanation by explaining complexities of similarities arising from the broader historical context.
Example: Both medieval and 18th-century hospitals focused more on care than on cure, and both were largely funded by charity rather than by the state. Medieval hospitals were run by religious orders and provided food, shelter, warmth, and prayer — only about 10% actually treated the sick. Similarly, 18th-century hospitals were funded by wealthy patrons and public subscriptions, and while they admitted more sick patients, they still lacked effective treatments because germ theory had not yet been discovered. Both types of hospital also refused to admit patients with infectious diseases to protect other residents. This continuity reflects the fact that without understanding what caused disease, hospitals could not offer real cures in either period.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of similarities. Students move from simple explanation by developed reasoning considering two or more identified similarities.
Example: Both medieval and 18th-century hospitals were charitable institutions rather than state-funded. Medieval hospitals were run by monks and nuns, while 18th-century hospitals were funded by wealthy donors. Both also focused on providing care rather than cure — medieval hospitals offered food, shelter, and prayer, while 18th-century hospitals still lacked effective treatments for most diseases.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of one similarity. Students move from basic explanation by reasoning supported with factual knowledge.
Example: Both medieval and 18th-century hospitals were funded by charity, not the government. Medieval hospitals were run by religious orders, while 18th-century hospitals relied on wealthy patrons and public donations.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of similarity/similarities. Students identify similarity/similarities relevant to the question. Explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Both types of hospital looked after sick people and were run by charities.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which surgery in the Middle Ages and surgery at the time of John Hunter were similar.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain two similarities
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of similarities. Students move from developed explanation by explaining complexities of similarities arising from the broader historical context.
Example: Both periods faced the same three fundamental problems of surgery — pain, infection, and bleeding — and in both periods, surgery remained a last resort. In the Middle Ages, barber surgeons used alcohol, opium sponges, or simply restrained patients during operations, while in Hunter’s time (18th century), surgeons still relied on speed and crude restraint because effective anaesthetics had not been developed. Infection was a problem in both periods because germ theory was not understood until the 1860s: medieval surgeons believed in ‘laudable pus’, and 18th-century surgeons still operated in dirty conditions with unwashed instruments. This continuity shows that until the key scientific breakthroughs of the 19th century (anaesthetics in 1846, antiseptic surgery in 1867), surgery remained fundamentally dangerous.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of similarities. Students move from simple explanation by developed reasoning considering two or more identified similarities.
Example: Both medieval surgeons and John Hunter faced the problem of pain during surgery. Medieval barber surgeons sometimes used opium or alcohol, and Hunter’s era still had no reliable anaesthetics. Both also struggled with infection — medieval surgeons had no knowledge of germs and believed pus was healthy, while surgeons in Hunter’s time still operated without sterilising instruments because germ theory had not been discovered.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of one similarity. Students move from basic explanation by reasoning supported with factual knowledge.
Example: Both medieval and 18th-century surgery faced the problem of infection. Medieval surgeons did not understand germs and believed in ‘laudable pus’. Surgeons in John Hunter’s time still did not know about germs, so instruments were not sterilised.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of similarity/similarities. Students identify similarity/similarities relevant to the question. Explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: Both periods had problems with pain and infection during surgery.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Has war been the main factor in the development of medicine in Britain? Explain your answer with reference to war and other factors. Use a range of examples from across your study of Health and the people: c1000 to the present day.
practice_questions.type: 16 marks (+4 SPaG) — Has war been the main factor?
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (13-16): Complex explanation of stated factor and other factor(s) leading to sustained judgement. Range of accurate and detailed knowledge. Complex, sustained line of reasoning, sharply focused and fully substantiated. Students develop by analysis of relationship between factors.
Example: War has been an important factor at several points but was not consistently the main driver across the whole period. In the medieval era, the Wars of the Roses gave barber surgeons decades of practice treating battlefield injuries, driving practical surgical improvement. Paré’s discovery of a better wound treatment came on the battlefield when he ran out of hot oil. WWI produced major advances including mobile X-ray units, blood transfusion techniques, and the Thomas splint for broken legs. WWII drove the mass production of penicillin when the US government funded Florey and Chain’s work. However, war only accelerated existing discoveries — it did not create new theoretical understanding. Germ theory, the Four Humours, and vaccination all developed outside wartime. Science and technology was the more consistent factor across the whole period.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Developed explanation of stated factor and other factor(s). Range of accurate knowledge. Developed, sustained line of reasoning. May suggest one factor has greater merit.
Example (stated factor): War drove surgical progress. Medieval barber surgeons gained most of their experience treating battlefield wounds. Paré discovered his healing balm as a French army surgeon. WWI produced mobile X-ray units, blood transfusions, and the Thomas splint. WWII led to mass production of penicillin.
Example (other factor): Individuals were also important regardless of war. Vesalius corrected over 300 of Galen’s anatomical errors through human dissection in 1543. Harvey proved blood circulates in 1628. Pasteur developed germ theory in 1861. Jenner pioneered vaccination in 1796. None of these breakthroughs were driven by war.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Simple explanation of stated factor or other factor(s). Specific knowledge. Simple, sustained line of reasoning.
Example: War helped surgery improve because barber surgeons gained experience treating wounds on the battlefield. The Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) gave over 30 years of practice amputating limbs, extracting arrows, and cauterising wounds.
Lower band (1-4): Basic explanation of one or more factors. Basic knowledge.
Example: War helped because surgeons got more practice treating injured soldiers.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks (+4 SPaG) — Has the role of the individual been the main factor?
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (13-16): Complex explanation of stated factor and other factor(s) leading to sustained judgement. Range of accurate and detailed knowledge. Complex, sustained line of reasoning, sharply focused and fully substantiated. Students develop by analysis of relationship between factors.
Example: Individuals were crucial in driving surgical progress at every stage, but they always depended on other factors. In the medieval period, Abulcasis invented 26 surgical instruments and popularised cauterisation, while Hugh and Theodoric of Lucca challenged the belief in ‘laudable pus’ by cleaning wounds with wine. John of Arderne used opium for pain relief and helped professionalise surgery through the Guild of Surgeons. Paré discovered his wound balm by chance and promoted ligatures. In the 19th century, Simpson introduced chloroform anaesthesia (1847), Lister developed antiseptic surgery (1867), and in the 20th century, Barnard performed the first heart transplant (1967). However, these individuals could only succeed because of enabling factors: war gave Paré battlefield experience, technology gave Lister carbolic acid, and government funding enabled mass production of penicillin. Individuals were essential but not sufficient alone.
Upper-mid band (9-12): Developed explanation of stated factor and other factor(s). Range of accurate knowledge. Developed, sustained line of reasoning. May suggest one factor has greater merit.
Example (stated factor): Individuals drove key breakthroughs in surgery. Abulcasis invented 26 new instruments and wrote a 30-volume surgical encyclopaedia. Paré replaced cauterisation with a soothing balm and introduced ligatures. Lister developed antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid in 1867, dramatically reducing infection.
Example (other factor): Science and technology was also vital. Without germ theory (Pasteur, 1861), Lister could not have understood why antiseptics worked. Without anaesthetics (ether 1846, chloroform 1847), complex surgery was impossible. Without blood transfusion technology, patients could not survive major operations.
Lower-mid band (5-8): Simple explanation of stated factor or other factor(s). Specific knowledge. Simple, sustained line of reasoning.
Example: Individuals were important because Paré improved surgery by discovering that a mixture of egg yolk, rose oil, and turpentine healed wounds better than cauterisation with boiling oil. He also introduced ligatures to tie off blood vessels after amputation.
Lower band (1-4): Basic explanation of one or more factors. Basic knowledge.
Example: Individuals like Paré and Lister made important changes to surgery.

lessons.title: Public Health & the Black Death
lessons.description: Filthy medieval towns, monastery sanitation, and the devastating arrival of the Black Death in 1348.
lessons.content_html:
Public Health in Medieval Towns

Medieval towns were unhealthy and unpleasant. Rapid growth, no scientific knowledge, and weak local governments meant most towns faced serious public health problems. These conditions set the stage for the Black Death in 1348.

The Key Problems

Most medieval towns faced the same problems:

Key Fact — Public Health Problems in Towns
  • Waste: There were no proper sewer systems. Household rubbish and human waste were thrown into the streets or dumped into rivers. Cesspits overflowed regularly and contaminated the surrounding area.
  • Water: Wells and rivers were often contaminated by nearby cesspits and industrial waste from butchers, tanners, and dyers. There was no understanding that dirty water could spread disease.
  • Overcrowding: Cramped, smoky houses packed closely together helped spread diseases like tuberculosis. Families often shared single rooms, and ventilation was poor.
  • Animals: Livestock were kept within town walls and animal waste added to the filth. Butchers slaughtered animals in the streets and dumped offal in open areas.

The main reasons were no scientific knowledge and weak local governments. People did not know about germs. They believed bad smells — miasma — caused disease. Town councils had limited power and money to enforce public health rules.

Attempts at Improvement

Medieval towns were not completely lawless. Town councils did try to manage the filth, even if their efforts were often small-scale and inconsistent:

Fines: Councils fined people for dumping waste in the street. But enforcement was patchy and fines were often too small to stop it.

Muck-rakers: Some towns hired muck-rakers to clear the worst rubbish. Their work was limited and could not keep up with the constant dumping.

Gong farmers: Gong farmers were paid to empty cesspits and privies, usually at night — one of the worst jobs in medieval society.

Water supply: Some towns provided clean water through conduits and maintained public wells. London’s Great Conduit (1236) carried fresh water from springs outside the city.

Public bathhouses: Available in some towns, though they declined over time due to fears about spreading disease and immorality.

Key Fact — Specific Public Health Laws
  • 1298: King Edward I ordered public toilets to be built in York because conditions were too unhygienic for his soldiers.
  • 1330: Glamorgan council banned butchers from throwing waste onto streets.
  • 1371: London banned the killing of large animals within the city.
  • 1388: Parliament passed a law fining people £20 (equivalent to roughly £15,000 today) for throwing waste into rivers.

These laws show that authorities were aware of the problems and tried to act — but enforcement was difficult and the measures were rarely enough to make a significant difference.

Monasteries: The Exception

Unlike filthy towns, monasteries were often the cleanest and healthiest places in medieval Britain. Monks had the resources and discipline to create public health systems far ahead of anything in towns.

Key Fact — Why Were Monasteries So Clean?
  • Wealth and knowledge: Monasteries had the money and education to build advanced water and sanitation systems. They could afford to plan and maintain infrastructure.
  • Excellent sanitation: They built latrines (toilets) that carried waste away through drainage channels, keeping it separate from their water supply.
  • Fresh water: Many monasteries had piped water supplies, using lead or wooden pipes to bring clean water from springs directly into the monastery grounds.
  • Routine and hygiene: The monastic rule required regular washing, clean clothing, and organised daily routines. This discipline helped maintain high standards of cleanliness.
  • Healthcare facilities: Monasteries had infirmaries for sick monks, herb gardens for growing medicinal plants, and access to medical texts preserved in their libraries.

This contrast shows that the knowledge and resources existed to create better public health — but most towns lacked the money, authority, and organisation to do it.

The Black Death (1348–1350)

The Black Death was the most catastrophic event in medieval history. It arrived in England in summer 1348 and swept across the country at terrifying speed. By 1350, it had killed one-third to one-half of England’s population — an estimated 1.5 to 2.5 million people. We now know it was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas on rats — but medieval people had no knowledge of this.

How Did It Arrive?

The Black Death started in Central Asia and spread west along trade routes. It reached Europe on merchant ships carrying infected rats and fleas. The disease arrived at Melcombe Regis (now Weymouth) in Dorset in June 1348 and spread rapidly through England over the next two years.

Europe was already weakened before the plague arrived. Poor harvests in the five years before 1348 had left much of the population malnourished and vulnerable. When the plague struck, weakened immune systems meant people had even less ability to fight it off.

Types and Symptoms

The Black Death took two main forms:

Key Fact — Two Forms of Plague
  • Bubonic plague: Spread by flea bites from infected rats. Symptoms included painful swollen lumps in the groin, armpits, or neck (called buboes), high fever, headaches, vomiting, and a rash of dark blotches on the skin. Around 60–70% of those infected died, usually within a week.
  • Pneumonic plague: Attacked the lungs and was spread through coughing and sneezing. This form was even more contagious and almost always fatal, often killing within 24–48 hours. Victims coughed up blood and struggled to breathe.

What Did People Believe Caused It?

Without knowledge of germs, people desperately searched for explanations:

Attempted Treatments and Prevention

People tried many methods to prevent or cure the plague, all based on their mistaken beliefs about its causes:

Flagellants: Groups of flagellants travelled town to town, publicly whipping themselves to beg God to end the plague. The Pope eventually condemned the movement.

Carrying posies and herbs: People carried flowers, herbs, and spices to ward off “bad air.” Some held vinegar-soaked cloths over their noses.

Bloodletting and purging: Physicians applied standard humoral treatments — bleeding patients and prescribing laxatives. These were completely useless against plague.

Quarantine: Some towns tried quarantine, boarding up infected houses or refusing entry to travellers from affected areas. This was one of the few measures that actually worked.

Prayer and processions: Churches held special services and masses to beg God for mercy. Many people made pilgrimages to holy shrines.

Fires and bells: Some believed smoke or vibrations from church bells could drive off the miasma.

The Impact of the Black Death

The Black Death had consequences far beyond the death toll itself:

1348–1350

The Black Death kills between one-third and one-half of England’s population

An estimated 1.5–2.5 million people died. Some villages were completely wiped out. Labour became desperately scarce.

1349 onwards

Labour shortage transforms society

With so many dead, surviving peasants could demand higher wages and better conditions. Some left their manors to find better-paid work elsewhere, weakening the feudal system.

1351

Statute of Labourers

The government attempted to freeze wages at pre-plague levels and prevent peasants from leaving their manors. This caused widespread resentment and was largely unenforceable.

1361, 1369, 1375

Plague returns repeatedly

The Black Death was not a one-off event. It returned in waves throughout the 14th century and beyond, continuing to disrupt society and reinforce the belief that disease was God’s punishment.

Short-term: The immediate response was mostly religious — prayer, flagellation, and persecution of minorities. Some practical steps were taken: quarantine, mass plague pits, street cleaning. But the scale of death overwhelmed any organised response.

Long-term: The plague forced people to question why traditional remedies and prayer had failed. It did not change medical theory overnight, but it planted seeds of doubt. The huge labour shortage shifted power from landowners to peasants, and some towns began taking public health more seriously. Repeated outbreaks also led to quarantine developing as a public health measure.

Impact on the Church: Prayer had failed to stop the plague, weakening the Church’s authority. Many priests died, leaving parishes without leadership. Some people began questioning whether the Church had all the answers — though this shift was gradual and would not fully develop until the Renaissance and Reformation.

When plague returned to London in 1665 — over 300 years later — people still did not know the real cause. The responses were very similar to 1348, showing how little understanding had changed.

London authorities issued “Plague Orders” that included a range of measures:

  • Quarantine of infected houses: Homes where plague was found were locked shut for 40 days, with a red cross painted on the door and a watchman posted outside to prevent anyone leaving.
  • Killing stray dogs and cats: Authorities ordered the slaughter of stray animals, ironically removing some of the very creatures that killed the rats carrying the disease.
  • Banning large gatherings: Public events and meetings were restricted to limit the spread of infection.
  • Burning infected clothes and bedding: Belongings of plague victims were destroyed in an attempt to stop the disease spreading.
  • Women “searchers”: Women were paid to examine the sick and the dead, identifying plague cases so that households could be quarantined.

The Great Plague of 1665 killed about 100,000 people in London — roughly a quarter of the city. Three centuries apart, the two outbreaks show a striking pattern: without understanding Yersinia pestis and how it spread, people relied on the same measures — quarantine, prayer, and trying to purify the air.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Don’t describe medieval towns as completely filthy with no rules. For top marks, show nuance: acknowledge the serious problems, but give specific examples of attempts to improve — gong farmers, fines, conduits. When writing about the Black Death, don’t just list the horrors — explain why people responded the way they did, linking responses to their beliefs about what caused disease.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

Medieval towns were unhealthy due to contaminated water, street waste, and overcrowding — but not completely lawless. Efforts like muck-rakers and fines show people did try. Monasteries proved better public health was possible with resources and organisation. The Black Death of 1348 was a turning point — its catastrophic death toll exposed the limits of existing medical knowledge and began to weaken trust in traditional remedies and Church authority.

Key Takeaways

  • Medieval towns had serious public health problems: Contaminated water, street waste, overcrowding, and miasma theory all contributed. But councils did try to improve conditions — showing this balance matters for top marks.
  • The Black Death killed one-third to one-half of England’s population: Arriving in 1348, people blamed God, miasma, planets, and minority groups. Only quarantine had any real effect.
  • Long-term consequences were significant: The plague weakened the feudal system, damaged Church authority, and encouraged people to question traditional medicine — laying groundwork for the Renaissance.

practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Explain the significance
practice_questions.marks:
All relevant and accurate points should be credited.
Top band (7-8): Complex explanation of aspects of significance. Answer demonstrates specific knowledge and understanding. Students move from developed explanation by explaining the relationship between aspects of significance, for example over time.
Example: The Black Death was significant both in its immediate impact and its long-term consequences for medicine. In the short term, it killed between one-third and one-half of England’s population (1348–1350), overwhelming all existing medical responses. Treatments based on the Four Humours (bloodletting, purging) were completely useless, and religious responses like flagellation and prayer also failed. Over time, this was highly significant because the failure of both rational and supernatural medicine planted seeds of doubt. The Church’s authority weakened when prayer failed to stop the plague, contributing to a gradual shift towards questioning traditional ideas. The development of quarantine during plague outbreaks was one of the first practical public health measures and became a lasting approach to epidemic control. The Black Death was therefore a turning point that began — very slowly — to undermine medieval medical orthodoxy.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of aspects of significance. Students move from simple explanation by developed reasoning considering two or more aspects of significance.
Example: The Black Death was significant because it exposed the limits of medieval medicine. Treatments based on the Four Humours, such as bloodletting and purging, were completely ineffective against plague. It was also significant for the Church’s authority: people had relied on prayer and pilgrimage, but these failed to stop the plague, weakening trust in religious explanations of disease.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Simple explanation of one aspect of significance. Students move from basic explanation by simple reasoning of one identified aspect.
Example: The Black Death was significant because it killed so many people that it created a labour shortage. Surviving peasants could demand higher wages, weakening the feudal system.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation of aspect(s) of significance. Students identify aspect(s) relevant to the question. Explanation likely implicit or by assertion.
Example: The Black Death was significant because it killed a lot of people in 1348.

Example: Both the Black Death and cholera epidemics were blamed on miasma (‘bad air’). During the Black Death, people carried posies and herbs. During cholera outbreaks, authorities tried to clean up smells, not realising the real cause was contaminated water.

Cholera led to the Public Health Acts (1848, 1875) and John Snow’s discovery that contaminated water spread the disease (1854). Both epidemics were therefore significant catalysts for public health reform, even when the science was wrong.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Developed explanation of similarities. Students move from simple explanation by developed reasoning considering two or more identified similarities.
Example: Both the Black Death and cholera led to government action on public health. During the Black Death, some towns quarantined infected houses and parliament passed laws about waste disposal. lessons.title: Vesalius, Paré & Harvey
lessons.description: Three Renaissance rebels who proved Galen wrong — through dissection, battlefield surgery and experiments on circulation.
lessons.content_html:
Introduction: The Renaissance Rebels

For over a thousand years, the ancient Greek physician Galen dominated European medicine. Doctors read Galen’s books rather than investigating the body for themselves. During the Renaissance, a new spirit of enquiry encouraged people to challenge ancient authority and seek knowledge through direct observation. Three figures — Vesalius, Paré, and Harvey — led this revolution.

Key Fact

All three of these figures shared a common approach: they relied on practical observation and experimentation rather than blindly accepting the teachings of Galen. This was a fundamental shift in how medicine was practised and taught.

Andreas Vesalius: The Father of Anatomy

Andreas Vesalius was a Belgian anatomist who transformed our understanding of the human body. He believed successful surgery required proper knowledge of anatomy. Most professors sat reading Galen’s texts while a barber-surgeon did the cutting. Vesalius carried out dissections himself on the bodies of executed criminals.

By studying human anatomy in detail, Vesalius proved that Galen — who had only dissected animals like monkeys and pigs — had made over 300 mistakes. For example, Vesalius showed that the human jawbone is one bone, not two as Galen had claimed.

In 1543, Vesalius published his groundbreaking book, ‘De Humani Corporis Fabrica’ (On the Fabric of the Human Body). It contained detailed, accurate drawings of the human body based on his own dissections.

The printing press spread his work across Europe, correcting centuries of error. For the first time, doctors across the continent could learn accurate anatomy.

Key Fact — Vesalius

Vesalius proved Galen wrong in over 300 places. His 1543 book, ‘On the Fabric of the Human Body’, used detailed illustrations from real human dissections. The printing press spread his corrected anatomy across Europe.

William Harvey: The Circulation Expert

William Harvey was an English doctor who challenged Galen’s theory that blood was made in the liver and “burned up” by the body. Through careful experiments and dissection, Harvey proved that blood circulates around the body in a continuous loop.

He demonstrated that the heart acts as a pump, forcing blood through the arteries and veins. He calculated the volume of blood pumped per heartbeat and showed it was far too much for the body to constantly produce and consume — it had to be the same blood going round and round.

Harvey published his work in 1628 in ‘An Anatomical Account of the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals’.

However, his discovery had little practical use at the time because blood transfusions were not yet possible. Without knowledge of blood groups, transfusions were very dangerous. It would be centuries before his discovery could save lives directly.

There was also a gap in Harvey’s theory: he could not explain how blood passed from arteries to veins. Microscopes of his time were too weak to reveal capillaries — the tiny vessels that complete the circuit. This gave opponents ammunition to attack his work, and he faced such ridicule that he went into semi-retirement. Capillaries were not found until after his death, when Marcello Malpighi identified them in 1661 using an improved microscope.

Key Fact — Harvey

Harvey proved that blood circulates around the body and that the heart acts as a pump. He published his findings in 1628. His work disproved Galen but had limited immediate practical impact because blood transfusions were not yet possible.

Ambroise Paré: The Father of Modern Surgery

Ambroise Paré was a French army surgeon who made big advances in surgical techniques. He regularly treated soldiers with gunshot wounds on the battlefield. The standard method was to burn wounds with boiling oil — a process called cauterisation — which was agonising for the patient.

One day, Paré ran out of hot oil and had to improvise. He made a soothing cream from egg yolk, rose oil, and turpentine. To his surprise, this was far less painful and helped wounds heal much better than cauterisation.

Paré also promoted silk threads called ligatures to tie off arteries after amputation, instead of burning the wound shut. This was much less painful.

However, ligatures carried a higher risk of infection because the threads could introduce germs into the wound. Without any understanding of germs or antiseptics, this was a serious drawback.

Paré also designed artificial limbs (prosthetics) for soldiers who had lost arms or legs in battle.

The King of France believed in the healing power of the Bezoar Stone — a stone from a goat’s stomach — which was widely believed to cure any poison.

Paré proposed a test. A condemned prisoner was offered a choice: die by hanging, or take a deadly poison and be treated with the Bezoar Stone. If he survived, he would go free. The prisoner chose the poison and the stone. He died in agony hours later, proving the stone had no healing power.

This grim experiment shows the Renaissance emphasis on testing ideas through observation rather than accepting traditional beliefs.

Key Fact — Paré

Paré discovered — by chance — that a mixture of egg yolk, rose oil, and turpentine was better than cauterisation for treating gunshot wounds. He also promoted ligatures instead of burning to stop bleeding after amputation, though this increased infection risk. He designed artificial limbs and used scientific testing to disprove superstitious remedies like the Bezoar Stone.

Why Were These Figures Significant?

You need to know not just what Vesalius, Paré, and Harvey discovered, but why their work mattered:

1543

Vesalius publishes On the Fabric of the Human Body

Proved Galen wrong in over 300 places. Established the principle that anatomy must be learned through human dissection, not ancient texts. The printing press spread his corrections across Europe.

1545 onwards

Paré develops new surgical techniques

Replaced cauterisation with a healing balm and promoted ligatures. Showed that chance observation and practical experience could improve medicine, even without formal theory.

1628

Harvey publishes his work on blood circulation

Proved the heart is a pump and blood circulates. Demonstrated that careful experimentation could overturn ideas accepted for over 1,000 years.

How Quickly Did Medicine Change?

Despite these breakthroughs, change was very slow. Their discoveries did not immediately transform everyday medical practice. In the hundred years after Paré’s death, thousands of people across Europe were still executed for witchcraft — a stark reminder that superstition remained deeply rooted, even as science was advancing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Don’t just list what Vesalius, Paré, and Harvey discovered. Explain why their work was significant — how it challenged old ideas, what factors helped them (e.g. the printing press, Renaissance thinking, chance), and what the limitations were.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

Vesalius, Paré, and Harvey moved medicine forward during the Renaissance. They challenged Galen’s teachings and showed that practical observation and experimentation mattered more than trusting ancient texts.

Key Takeaways

  • Vesalius corrected anatomy: He proved Galen wrong in over 300 places. His 1543 book, spread by the printing press, gave doctors accurate anatomy for the first time.
  • Paré improved surgery through chance: Running out of hot oil led him to a better wound treatment. He introduced ligatures, though infection remained a problem.
  • Harvey proved circulation: He showed blood circulates and the heart is a pump, disproving Galen. But practical benefits were limited until blood transfusions became possible centuries later.

lessons.title: Continuity & Change in Medicine
lessons.description: The 18th-century transition: quackery and miasma persisted, but the Enlightenment, new hospitals and John Hunter pushed medicine forward.
lessons.content_html:
Introduction: A Time of Transition

The 18th century was a time of transition for medicine in Britain. Vesalius, Paré, and Harvey had made important breakthroughs, but many old ideas about disease and treatment stubbornly persisted. This lesson looks at what stayed the same (continuity) and what was genuinely new (change) in how people understood and treated disease.

What Stayed the Same (Continuity)

Even though science was becoming more important, many old ideas about disease were still popular among ordinary people.

Key Fact — Persistent Old Beliefs
  • Miasma — the belief that “bad air” or foul smells caused illness — was still widely accepted.
  • The ancient Greek idea of the Four Humours had not disappeared entirely.
  • Many people still believed that illness was a punishment from God.

The Medical “Marketplace”

For most people, healthcare in the 1600s–1700s was like a marketplace — they could choose between different practitioners, none of whom were reliably effective:

Key Fact — Who Could You Visit for Medical Help?
  • Barber-surgeons: Poorly trained practitioners who gave haircuts and performed minor operations like tooth-pulling and bloodletting. Surgery was seen as a low-status craft.
  • Apothecaries: Sold medicines and potions, often with little formal training. They were the forerunners of modern pharmacists and often the only medical help for poorer people.
  • Wise women: Used traditional knowledge of herbs and plants, sometimes mixed with superstition. Often the first point of contact for rural communities.
  • Quack doctors: Travelling salesmen who sold fake “cure-all” medicines. There was no regulation to stop them, and desperate people were easy targets.

The lack of regulation meant medical treatment was very inconsistent. Wealthy patients could afford physicians, but even physicians often relied on outdated ideas like bloodletting and purging.

New Treatments from Overseas

As European exploration expanded in the 16th and 17th centuries, new treatments arrived from abroad:

  • Quinine from South American tree bark was used to treat malaria and was one of the first genuinely effective imported medicines.
  • Opium was used as a powerful painkiller, though it caused serious addiction.
  • Tobacco was believed to be a cure-all for almost every illness — a claim since disproved.

Supernatural Beliefs Persisted

Even as new scientific ideas spread, supernatural beliefs remained widespread. Many people believed in the King’s Touch — the idea that the monarch’s touch could cure scrofula (a form of tuberculosis known as the “King’s Evil”). Thousands attended royal ceremonies hoping to be healed. This shows how slowly scientific thinking replaced superstition.

What Was New (Change)

The 18th century was part of the Enlightenment, when science and reason were becoming very important. This spirit of enquiry began to influence medicine.

Key Fact — Key Changes in the 18th Century
  • The growth of hospitals: Before, hospitals were mostly places of “care” run by the Church. New hospitals were now built with the aim of curing patients.
  • Doctors trained in hospitals: Physicians began observing patients in wards, learning through direct experience rather than only from books.
  • Free dispensaries: Set up for the poor, these provided medicine and advice without requiring payment for a doctor’s visit.

Case Study: John Hunter (1728–1793)

John Hunter shows the new scientific approach to medicine. Often called the “Father of Scientific Surgery”, he pushed a new way of thinking about medical practice.

Instead of accepting old ideas from books, Hunter taught that surgeons must learn through observation and experiment. He was a skilled anatomist who carried out many dissections to understand how the body worked.

Hunter collected thousands of anatomical specimens (preserved body parts, organs, and bones) in a museum at his home. He used these to teach students with hands-on experience rather than just textbook lectures.

He experimented on himself and on animals, studying how diseases progressed and how the body healed. He improved techniques for treating wounds and aneurysms, helping turn surgery from a simple craft into a respected science.

His collection later became the basis of the Hunterian Museum at the Royal College of Surgeons in London.

Hunter’s Surgical Innovations

One of Hunter’s most celebrated achievements was treating a popliteal aneurysm — a dangerously swollen artery behind the knee. The standard treatment was amputation, which was brutal and often fatal. Hunter tied off the artery higher up the leg, allowing other blood vessels to expand and keep the leg alive. This showed his approach in action: observe the problem, hypothesise a solution, test it.

Getting bodies for dissection was a major problem. Henry VIII had granted surgeons just 4 hanged criminals per year for anatomical study. As demand grew, this was hopelessly inadequate.

The result was a grim trade in stolen corpses. “Resurrection men” stole fresh bodies from graves and sold them to surgeons and medical schools. Hunter himself obtained bodies this way — many surgeons saw it as a necessary evil.

Hunter was so dedicated that he deliberately infected himself with a sexually transmitted disease to study its effects. This was an extreme and dangerous example of his belief that direct observation was the only way to truly understand disease.

He also ran a large medical practice, trained hundreds of students, and wrote influential books on dentistry, gunshot wounds, and venereal diseases. His teaching shaped a generation of surgeons who spread his evidence-based methods.

Hunter and the Professionalisation of Surgery

Hunter argued that surgeons and barbers should be separated and that surgery should become a respected profession, not a trade practised by people who also cut hair. His campaigning helped establish the Royal College of Surgeons in 1800, which still oversees surgery in England today.

Key Fact — John Hunter

John Hunter promoted observation and experiment over reliance on old textbooks. He collected thousands of anatomical specimens to teach students, pioneered new surgical techniques (including tying off aneurysms instead of amputating), and helped establish surgery as a respected profession through the Royal College of Surgeons. His methods helped transform surgery into a respected, evidence-based science.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about this period, discuss both continuity and change. A good answer shows that you understand progress was not straightforward — old beliefs like miasma and the Four Humours persisted even as new ideas emerged. A balanced answer covering both sides will score higher marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Conclusion

The 18th century was a time of transition. New scientific thinking was taking hold — especially through figures like John Hunter — but most people still relied on old beliefs and traditional remedies. Real, widespread change would not come until the 19th century.

Key Takeaways

  • Old beliefs persisted: Miasma, the Four Humours, and supernatural explanations remained common, alongside quackery and herbal remedies.
  • New institutions emerged: Hospitals shifted from care to cure, doctors trained through observation, and free dispensaries helped the poor.
  • John Hunter bridged old and new: He championed observation and experimentation, helping transform surgery into a respected, evidence-based profession.
